title: Secondary Cells and Accumulators
short_intro: Secondary cells are electrochemical storage devices that can be electrically recharged after discharge by passing current in the reverse direction. They function based on reversible redox reactions, allowing repeated cycles of conversion between chemical and electrical energy.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Working principle of secondary cells, lead-acid accumulator, EMF and internal resistance, terminal potential difference, grouping of cells.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Faraday's laws of electrolysis applied to charging/discharging, capacity of accumulators (Ampere-hour efficiency), internal resistance variation with state of charge, thermodynamic considerations of reversible cells.

concept_notes.heading: Principle of Secondary Cells
bullets: Secondary cells act as galvanic (voltaic) cells during discharge, converting chemical energy into electrical energy.
They act as electrolytic cells during charging, where an external DC source drives non-spontaneous reverse chemical reactions.
The reversibility of the chemical reactions is the defining characteristic that permits multiple cycles of use.

concept_notes.heading: Lead-Acid Accumulator Structure
bullets: The positive plate consists of lead dioxide (PbO<sub>2</sub>) and the negative plate consists of spongy lead (Pb).
The electrolyte is an aqueous solution of sulfuric acid (H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>) with a specific gravity of approximately 1.250 to 1.280 when fully charged.
Separators made of porous insulating material prevent direct short-circuiting between adjacent positive and negative plates.

concept_notes.heading: Chemical Reactions during Discharge and Charge
bullets: At the anode (negative plate during discharge): Pb + SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup> → PbSO<sub>4</sub> + 2e<sup>-</sup>.
At the cathode (positive plate during discharge): PbO<sub>2</sub> + 4H<sup>+</sup> + SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup> + 2e<sup>-</sup> → PbSO<sub>4</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O.
Overall discharge reaction: Pb + PbO<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> ⇒ 2PbSO<sub>4</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O, which reverses during charging.

concept_notes.heading: Characteristics and Efficiency
bullets: Internal resistance of secondary cells is extremely low (typically a fraction of an ohm), allowing them to deliver very high surge currents.
Ampere-hour (Ah) efficiency is defined as the ratio of discharge current multiplied by discharge time to charging current multiplied by charging time, typically ranging from 80% to 90%.
Energy efficiency is always lower than Ah efficiency due to the higher cell voltage during charging compared to discharging.

derivations.title: Terminal Potential Difference During Charging and Discharging
derivations.conditions: Cell of EMF E and internal resistance r connected in an external circuit.
steps: During discharge, current I flows out of the positive terminal. By Ohm's law, the potential drop across internal resistance is Ir.
The terminal potential difference V is given by V = E - Ir.
During charging, current I is forced into the positive terminal by an external source. The potential drop adds to the EMF.
The terminal potential difference during charging becomes V = E + Ir.
derivations.result: Discharge: V = E - Ir; Charge: V = E + Ir

derivations.title: Power Transfer and Maximum Power Theorem for a Secondary Cell
derivations.conditions: Cell of EMF E and internal resistance r connected to external load resistance R.
steps: Circuit current is given by I = E / (R + r).
Power P delivered to the external load is P = I<sup>2</sup>R = E<sup>2</sup>R / (R + r)<sup>2</sup>.
To find the condition for maximum power, differentiate P with respect to R and set dP/dR = 0.
Differentiating yields (R + r)<sup>2</sup> - 2R(R + r) = 0, which simplifies to R = r.
derivations.result: Maximum power is transferred to the load when external resistance equals internal resistance (R = r).

graphs_and_experiments.title: Discharge Curve of a Secondary Cell
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Plot of terminal voltage V (y-axis) versus discharge time t (y-axis) showing an initial rapid drop, a long plateau, and a steep final fall.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The long flat region indicates stable operating voltage due to constant chemical composition of active materials. The sharp drop marks exhaustion of H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Questions testing the behavior of terminal voltage over time and identification of the plateau region.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Specific Gravity vs. State of Charge
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Linear or near-linear curve of electrolyte specific gravity (y-axis) against state of charge percentage (x-axis) ranging from 1.100 (discharged) to 1.280 (charged).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: As H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is consumed during discharge, density of electrolyte decreases directly reflecting the state of charge.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Hydrometer test principles used in practical physics and conceptual questions.

graphs_and_experiments.title: V-I Characteristic Graph for a Secondary Cell
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Straight line plot of terminal potential V against current I, starting at V = E when I = 0 and sloping downwards for discharge (V = E - Ir) and upwards for charging (V = E + Ir).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The intercept on the voltage axis gives the EMF E, and the slope of the line magnitude represents the internal resistance r.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Graphical determination of EMF and internal resistance in experimental physics problems.

solved_numericals.question: A storage battery of EMF 12 V and internal resistance 0.5 \Omega is being charged by a DC source of 20 V using a series resistor of 1.5 \Omega. Find the charging current and the terminal potential difference of the battery.
solution_steps: Identify the total EMF in opposition: Source EMF = 20 V, Battery EMF = 12 V.
Total resistance in the circuit: R_total = R_external + r = 1.5 \Omega + 0.5 \Omega = 2.0 \Omega.
Calculate charging current: I = (V_source - E_battery) / R_total = (20 - 12) / 2.0 = 8 / 2 = 4 A.
Calculate terminal potential difference during charging: V = E + Ir = 12 + (4 \times 0.5) = 12 + 2 = 14 V.
solved_numericals.answer: Charging current = 4 A, Terminal potential difference = 14 V

solved_numericals.question: A lead-acid accumulator has an ampere-hour capacity of 100 Ah. If it is discharged at a constant current of 5 A for 16 hours and subsequently charged at 10 A for 9 hours, calculate its ampere-hour efficiency and energy efficiency assuming average discharging and charging voltages of 1.9 V and 2.3 V respectively.
solution_steps: Calculate discharge output (Ah_out) = I_d \times t_d = 5 \text{ A} \times 16 \text{ h} = 80 \text{ Ah}.
Calculate charge input (Ah_in) = I_c \times t_c = 10 \text{ A} \times 9 \text{ h} = 90 \text{ Ah}.
Calculate energy output (E_out) = V_d \times Ah_out = 1.9 \text{ V} \times 80 \text{ Ah} = 152 \text{ Wh}.
Calculate energy input (E_in) = V_c \times Ah_in = 2.3 \text{ V} \times 90 \text{ Ah} = 207 \text{ Wh}.

solved_numericals.question: A secondary cell gives a balancing length of 70 cm on a potentiometer wire. When the cell is short-circuited through a 2 \Omega resistor, the balancing length falls to 50 cm. Find the internal resistance of the cell.
solution_steps: Potentiometer balancing length is directly proportional to potential difference: l_1 \propto E and l_2 \propto V.
Relation between EMF and terminal voltage with external resistance R: E / V = l_1 / l_2.
Use internal resistance formula: r = R ((E / V) - 1).

assumptions_and_limitations: Internal resistance is assumed to be constant during moderate discharge cycles, although in reality, it increases as the specific gravity of the sulfuric acid decreases and lead sulfate accumulates on the plates.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Terminal voltage of a secondary cell is always equal to its EMF regardless of operating conditions.
common_misconceptions.correct: Terminal voltage equals EMF only when no current is drawn (open circuit). It is V = E - Ir during discharge and V = E + Ir during charge.
common_misconceptions.why: Internal resistance causes an internal potential drop proportional to the current flowing through the cell.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Charging a secondary cell increases its internal resistance permanently.
common_misconceptions.correct: Charging restores the chemical composition of the active plates and electrolyte, thereby reducing the internal resistance back to its normal low state.
common_misconceptions.why: Reversible electrochemical reactions regenerate the original low-resistance reactants (Pb, PbO<sub>2</sub>, and strong H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>).

quick_revision: Secondary cells are rechargeable cells utilizing reversible redox reactions like the lead-acid accumulator.
Discharging Terminal Voltage: V = E - Ir
Charging Terminal Voltage: V = E + Ir
